claims.text: The starting material consists of mixed precursors for more than five noble-metal-based elements, in nanoparticle, salt, oxidized, or dispersed form before reduction.
Single-phase formation is governed by precursor-reduction kinetics and subsequent atomic diffusion.
An intermediate annealing hold slows reduction of the noble-metal precursors.
Slower reduction gives constituent atoms enough time to diffusively homogenize.
The additional diffusion time relieves lattice strain and reduces defect trapping.
Reduced strain and defect trapping favor uniform nucleation of a single FCC or otherwise targeted solid-solution phase.
Rapid heating and cooling create a kinetically trapped state before full atomic mixing occurs.
Kinetic trapping causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology.
The controlled intervention is an intermediate heating hold followed by final heating and slow cooling, rather than one-step rapid heating and cooling.
The intermediate hold should occur near completion of precursor reduction while atomic mobility remains moderate and before rapid nucleation would otherwise occur.
The process should be conducted under an inert or reducing atmosphere.
Local lattice strain and defect density during nucleation influence atom incorporation and phase selection.
More uniform diffusion reduces local concentration gradients and enables formation of a common FCC lattice.
Relative to rapid processing, the controlled regime will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid processing, the controlled regime will produce a dominant single FCC or intended phase with more uniform lattice parameters and lower lattice strain.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles have higher thermal decomposition temperatures because of kinetic trapping and lattice strain.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when precursor reduction temperatures are not widely disparate and may fail when elemental reduction kinetics differ too greatly.
Thermodynamic instability can outweigh kinetic effects and prevent the proposed intervention from producing a single phase.

Failure of the annealed samples to show statistically significant improvements in phase purity and elemental homogeneity, together with a lower thermal decomposition temperature, would falsify the hypothesis.
